title: weapons in the shami tree
hookLine: a bundle tied high in a shami tree near the cremation ground, and nobody wants to go near it
carry: why hindus honor the shami and their tools

lines: A SHAMI TREE BY THE CREMATION GROUND.
cards: A shami tree stands near a cremation ground outside King Virata's city. Thick branches, hard to climb, and a place people would rather walk past. Nakula climbs it.
He ties a long bundle high in the branches, wrapped tight so the rain won't reach it. Inside is luggage that could end the whole disguise: Arjuna's bow, the Gandiva, and the brothers' other weapons.
A wandering cook can't carry a bow every warrior knows on sight. So the weapons stay behind.

teach.h: A BODY TO KEEP PEOPLE AWAY
teach.b: The text adds a grim, clever detail. To keep curious people away, the brothers tie a dead body in the tree too, and tell passing herdsmen it's an old family custom. Nobody climbs a tree like that.
Then they enter the city one at a time: Yudhishthira with dice wrapped in cloth, Bhima with a ladle, Arjuna in women's ornaments.
Draupadi walks the streets in one worn cloth until Queen Sudeshna calls her up, and when the queen worries the king will look at her, Draupadi says she has Gandharva husbands who guard her unseen.
It's true, in its way: they're in the kitchen, the stables and at the dice table. And the bundle stays in the tree for a year. Here's why Hindus still care.
The tree that kept the Pandavas' weapons is honored to this day.
In many regions, at Dussehra, also called Vijayadashami, families worship the shami tree, and in some places people trade its leaves as gold.
The popular telling links it to this story: the weapons coming back down at the year's end.
Around the same days, many families keep Ayudha Puja.

They clean and bless the tools of their work, books, a car, a laptop, a sewing machine, because in Hindu teaching work done rightly is an offering, and what serves it deserves respect. Today, look at what you work with.
A tool set aside isn't forgotten. It's waiting, honored, for its day.

how: In many regions the shami tree is worshipped at Dussehra (Vijayadashami), and popular tradition links the custom to the Pandavas' weapons; Ayudha Puja, the blessing of tools, is kept around the same days, especially in South India.

o: a heavenly being who guards a woman unseen
the tree where the Pandavas hide their weapons
the king whose city takes in the Pandavas in disguise

games.q: what each one carried into the city — tap the pairs.
p: a cook's ladle and a knife

s: the Pandavas carried their weapons into Virata's city
they tied them high in a shami tree near the cremation ground.
they entered the city one at a time
each came alone, so five strong men never arrived together.
Ayudha Puja means blessing only soldiers' weapons
families bless the tools of any work: books, cars, laptops, sewing machines.

games.q: it's Dussehra, and your aunt sets your laptop beside the family's tools for Ayudha Puja. what's the idea?
o: it's a charm so it won't crash.
work done rightly is an offering, so the tools that serve it are honored.
it's a polite way to make you take a day off.
games.why: the things that serve your work are treated with respect, the way the shami tree, which kept the Pandavas' weapons, is honored at Dussehra.

practice: If a tool of your work or study is nearby, a pen, a laptop, a phone, set it in front of you, the way families set out their tools at Ayudha Puja. Some mark them with a dot of kumkum or a flower; a simple thank-you is enough.
Breathing in, notice the work it helps you do. Breathing out, thank it, and the people your work serves. If you pray, you can offer that work in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Virata. The king who welcomes a dice player, a cook, a dance teacher, two herders and a maid, never guessing who they are.

orig.note: the Matsya king whose court shelters the Pandavas; the book of the epic is named for him.

carryVoice: Your line: why Hindus honor the shami and their tools. Weapons in a tree, waiting for their day. That's day eight hundred eight.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Pandava-pravesa), the weapons hidden in the shami tree and the Pandavas' arrival at Virata's court
Living practice: shami puja at Vijayadashami and Ayudha Puja at Navaratri, described in general terms; the link to the Pandavas is the popular telling
